newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU assembly says arms embargo on China must stay.
newsitem.headline: EU assembly says arms embargo on China must stay.

text.p: The European Parliament urged the European Union on Thursday to maintain its arms embargo against China, attacking Beijing's perceived abuse of human rights, but called for closer EU-China trade relations.
"The European Parliament sees no justification for the lifting of the EU arms embargo imposed on China in 1989," the parliament said in a report on future EU ties with China.
The ban was imposed after the 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
In a move likely to anger China, the parliament also repeated its demand for the EU's executive Commission to open an information bureau in Taiwan, Beijing's rival.

The EU's assembly went on to deplore China's dissolution of Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council, its "occupation of Tibet", its role in developing nuclear arms in Pakistan and supplying chemical weapons and missiles to Iran, and its support for Burma's military government.

At the same time the parliament recognised the commercial importance to European businesses of a Chinese market of 1.2 billion people and decided constructive engagement would be more profitable than trying to isolate Beijing.

Among their recommendations for constructive engagement, the assembly listed the creation of an office in Beijing to represent EU trade interests, negotiations on a wide-ranging trade accord and annual EU-China summits.

The assembly's report, drafted by British Conservative Edward McMillan Scott, delivered another snub to French President Jacques Chirac, who was openly attacked by Euro-MPs and EU Commissioner Hans van den Broek in May for blocking formal United Nations condemnation of China's rights record.

"The European Parliament insists on the need for the EU and its member states to closely coordinate their political and economic policies on China," the report said, suggesting that the 15-member EU bloc could start by drawing up a code of conduct for European companies operating in China.

China escaped formal condemnation from the UN Human Rights Commission in April after France broke with the EU's tradition of unanimously backing motions critical of Beijing. Germany, Greece, Italy and Spain followed suit.

The parliament attacked the move just as Chirac, then in the throes of an election campaign, arrived in China for a business mission which led to the signing of business deals worth hundreds of millions of dollars and set the seal on strong Sino-French political ties.
